extracted.intended_audience: people producing online math explainers (teachers, students, mathematicians, engineers, outreach creators)
extracted.subtask_description: Submitting a new math-focused explainer (video, blog post, interactive, etc.) to the 3Blue1Brown Summer of Math Exposition contest; entries will be judged for clarity, motivation, novelty, and memorability and must meet contest constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: New work created during the summer
rubrics_metrics.description: It has to be something new you make this summer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The spirit is to encourage people who've never put stuff online before. If you want to work on something you sort of started once before, that's probably fine, but it can't be something you already published before this contest. Optimally, you'd use this as a chance to try something new you otherwise might not have.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic must be about math (broadly defined)
rubrics_metrics.description: It has to be about math.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Math is meant very broadly; applied topics like physics or computer science are abundantly welcome. A viewer/reader should come away knowing something mathematical they didn't before.

rubrics_metrics.name: State assumed audience background if niche
rubrics_metrics.description: If you're assuming a certain background level for the target audience, kindly mention it below.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges may not fit niche expert audiences (e.g., algebraic geometry), so to actually win it's helpful if the topic is accessible to someone with ~standard undergrad math background. Mentioning required prerequisites helps set expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: One entry per person or group
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may make more projects, but the contest will judge participants based on a single entry due to capacity constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: English accessibility requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: It has to be available in English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explainers in other languages are welcome generally, but to be considered for this contest the lesson must be accessible to English-speaking judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicly visible and free
rubrics_metrics.description: It has to be publicly visible and available for people to consume for free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions must be freely accessible so judges and the public can view them without paywalls or restricted access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Jargon should be explained, the goals of the lesson should be understandable with minimal background, and the submission should generally display empathy for people unfamiliar with the topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize clear exposition: explain terms, state goals upfront, and structure so newcomers can follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation (hook within first 30 seconds)
rubrics_metrics.description: It should be clear to the reader/viewer within the first 30 seconds why they should care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Openings should quickly communicate relevance or intrigue to capture attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: It doesn't necessarily have to be an original idea or original topic, but it should offer someone an experience they might otherwise not have by searching around online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value can come from covering common topics in better ways or surfacing obscure ideas; aim to provide a distinct perspective or presentation rather than repeating existing material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorability
rubrics_metrics.description: Something should make the piece easy to remember even several months later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memorable elements include beauty of presentation, presenter enthusiasm, or an 'aha' moment. Consider distinctive visuals, narrative hooks, or surprising insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility of substance in short viewing
rubrics_metrics.description: For longer works, judges might not be able to consume the full video/post.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because selection is time-limited, the substance of your work should be clearly visible with a 5–10 minute view; ensure key ideas and value are accessible early or provide a concise synopsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-review pre-filter and ranking procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants may be asked to peer review some other participants' submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This would involve looking at five other entries and ranking them 1–5 based on how well they fit the criteria above; cumulative scoring from those rankings may be used to determine a manageable pre-filtered set for the judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-faith and non-offensive content
rubrics_metrics.description: This only applies to good faith submissions; anything irrelevant or offensive would not be included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions should be earnest, relevant to the contest goals, and not contain offensive material; such entries will be excluded from consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teams and group entries allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: Entries from groups or teams are welcomed and encouraged too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group submissions are permitted but still count as a single entry for that group under the one-entry rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target-audience accessibility expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: The contest aims to encourage broadly useful explainers and activation energy for creators who haven't published before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While niche advanced topics are allowed, creators should consider general accessibility or clearly label the intended expertise level; judges favor pieces that serve wider learning and outreach goals.
